title: Archives and SSH Essentials: tar, ssh-keygen, scp, rsync
summary: Quick revision notes on packing and compressing files with tar, gzip, xz and zip, then on SSH key authentication, ~/.ssh/config, key permissions, and moving files with scp and rsync.

chapters.title: Archives and Compression: The Mental Model
points: tar only bundles many files into one stream (an archive); it does not shrink them. Compression is a separate step layered on top, which is why names look like .tar.gz
gzip is fast with a good ratio and the default choice; xz compresses smaller but is slower; both compress one stream, so the usual form is tar plus gzip or xz
zip bundles and compresses each file separately in one format, so you can pull out a single file cheaply and it opens on Windows and macOS without extra tools
Comparison: .tar.gz = fast, universal on Linux; .tar.xz = smallest, slow; .zip = cross-platform, per-file access, does not keep Unix owner or permission details as reliably as tar
Mistake: expecting gzip alone to handle a folder; gzip compresses single files only, so wrap folders with tar first
Interview Point: Why is tar.gz called two tools in one? Why can you extract one file from zip faster than from tar.gz? When would you choose xz over gzip? Does tar compress by default?

chapters.title: tar: Create, List and Extract
points: Mode flags: c create, x extract, t list; add f for the archive filename (it must be the last flag in the cluster, directly before the name), and v for verbose
Create a gzip archive: tar -czf backup.tar.gz project/ ; create an xz archive: tar -cJf backup.tar.xz project/ (capital J is xz, lowercase z is gzip)
List without extracting: tar -tzf backup.tar.gz ; always list first when the archive comes from someone else
Extract into a chosen folder: tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -C /tmp/restore (the folder must already exist); extract one member: tar -xzf backup.tar.gz project/config.yml

Mistake: tar -czf project/ backup.tar.gz makes f take project/ as the archive name and can overwrite your source; always put the archive name right after f. Also, modern GNU tar auto-detects compression on extract, so tar -xf works for .gz and .xz
Interview Point: What do c, x, t, f, z and J each mean? How do you extract to a different directory? Why list an archive before extracting? What goes wrong if f is not followed by the filename?

chapters.title: gzip, xz and zip in Daily Use
points: gzip file.log replaces file.log with file.log.gz (the original is removed); keep it with gzip -k file.log ; undo with gunzip file.log.gz
xz works the same way: xz -k big.log makes big.log.xz and unxz big.log.xz restores it; levels run -0 (fast) to -9 (smallest), and -9 uses a lot of memory
Create zip recursively: zip -r site.zip site/ ; extract: unzip site.zip -d out/ ; list: unzip -l site.zip ; without -r, zip stores the folder entry but not its contents
Read a compressed file without extracting: zcat file.log.gz, zgrep ERROR file.log.gz, xzcat file.xz
Mistake: running gzip on a log you still need and being surprised the original is gone; and unzip into the current directory can scatter files, so use -d or list first
Interview Point: Why does gzip delete the original file? How do you keep it? How do you search inside a .gz without unpacking? What does zip -r add that plain zip does not?

chapters.title: SSH Keys: ed25519, authorized_keys and ssh-copy-id
points: Key pair: the private key stays on your machine and is never shared; the public key (.pub) goes on the server. SSH proves you hold the private key without sending it

Generate: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@laptop" ; this writes ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (private) and id_ed25519.pub (public); set a passphrase so a stolen file is not enough, and use ssh-agent plus ssh-add to avoid retyping it
Install the public key with ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub user@host ; it appends the key as one line to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server, one key per line
Comparison: ed25519 has short keys, is fast and is the modern default; RSA needs at least 3072 bits to be comparable; password login can be brute-forced and is disabled in hardened servers
Mistake: copying the private key to the server or pasting the wrong file; only the .pub contents go into authorized_keys. Test with ssh user@host before turning off password login
Interview Point: Which key goes on the server and which stays local? What does ssh-copy-id actually do? Why choose ed25519 over RSA? What is the passphrase protecting against?

chapters.title: ~/.ssh/config, Key Permissions, scp and rsync
points: ~/.ssh/config defines aliases: Host prod / HostName 203.0.113.10 / User deploy / Port 2222 / IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ; then ssh prod replaces the long command, and scp and rsync use the alias too

Permissions SSH enforces: ~/.ssh is 700, private key 600, authorized_keys 600 (or 644), config 600; if the private key is readable by others, ssh refuses with UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE, and the server ignores authorized_keys if the home or .ssh folder is writable by others

scp copies over SSH: scp file.txt prod:/tmp/ upload, scp prod:/var/log/app.log . download, scp -r dir/ prod:/srv/ for folders, and uppercase -P sets the port (ssh uses lowercase -p). It always copies everything again

rsync sends only the differences: rsync -avz --progress src/ prod:/srv/app/ ; -a keeps permissions and times and recurses, -z compresses in transit, and --delete mirrors by removing extra files on the destination, so dry-run it first with -n

Mistake: the trailing slash: src/ copies the contents of src, src without a slash copies the folder itself into the destination. Comparison: use scp for a one-off file, rsync for repeats, large trees and resuming interrupted transfers

Interview Point: What permissions must the private key and .ssh have, and what happens otherwise? How does the trailing slash change rsync? Why is rsync faster than scp on a second run? What does --delete do and how do you test it safely?

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Archives, SSH Keys, scp and rsync
points: tar: create tar -czf out.tar.gz dir/ | xz tar -cJf out.tar.xz dir/ | list tar -tzf out.tar.gz | extract tar -xzf out.tar.gz -C dest/
gzip -k f then gunzip f.gz | xz -k f then unxz f.xz | zip -r a.zip dir/ then unzip a.zip -d out/ | peek zcat, zgrep, xzcat
Keys: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "label" | ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub user@host | public key goes into server ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
Permissions: ~/.ssh 700, private key 600, authorized_keys 600, config 600 | config block: Host, HostName, User, Port, IdentityFile
Transfer: scp -r -P 2222 dir/ host:/path | rsync -avz --progress -n src/ host:/dest/ (drop -n to run) | trailing slash on src/ means contents only
